title: Routing and Default Gateways
oneLiner: How a PC decides whether a destination is local or must go to the router, and how a router picks the next hop: masks, the default gateway, routing tables and longest prefix match.
keyTakeaway: A host compares the destination with its own network using its mask: same network, deliver directly; different network, hand the packet to the default gateway. Routers then choose the most specific matching route (longest prefix wins), with the default route 0.0.0.0/0 catching everything else, one hop at a time.
explanation:
Routing is how packets find their way between networks. It starts on your own PC, which makes one decision for every packet: is the destination on my network? It ANDs its own address and the destination with its subnet mask; if the two network addresses match, the destination is local and the PC delivers the packet itself through the switch. If not, it sends the packet to its default gateway, the router interface on its own subnet whose address was set by hand or by DHCP.

A router keeps a routing table: a list of destination networks, each with the next hop to send matching packets to and the interface to use. Directly connected networks need no next hop. Other entries are typed in (static routes) or learned from neighbouring routers through routing protocols such as OSPF inside a company and BGP between internet providers. When several routes match, the most specific one wins: a /24 beats a /16, which beats the default route 0.0.0.0/0. This rule is called longest prefix match. Every router lowers the packet's TTL (time to live) by one, so a packet caught in a routing loop dies instead of circling forever; traceroute uses this to reveal each router on the path.

Most "I can reach local things but not the internet" problems are here: a wrong mask makes a remote host look local, so the PC tries ARP for it and gets no answer; a missing or mistyped gateway leaves no way off the subnet; and a gateway that isn't in the PC's own subnet can't be reached at all.
